record.paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
record.original_question: What experimental evidence can definitively establish that charge-ordered nanoclusters exist above the Curie temperature Tc in colossal-magnetoresistance manganites, rule out a homogeneous explanation of the CMR effect, and determine how those nanoclusters appear in optical-conductivity spectra rather than being described only as small polarons?

evidence.quote: The evidence for charge-ordered nanoclusters above TC should be further confirmed. It is important that a variety of techniques reach the same conclusions regarding the presence of nanoclusters above TC, definitely ruling out an homogeneous state as the cause of the CMR effect. For instance, it would be important to find out the role played by nanoclusters on optical conductivity results, which thus far has been described mainly as consisting of "small polarons" (Noh and collaborators). How do the nanoclusters manifest themselves in the optical spectra?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In hole-doped manganese perovskite oxides of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a trivalent rare-earth cation such as La, Pr, Nd and A a divalent alkaline-earth cation such as Ca, Sr, Ba) at doping concentrations x in the regime exhibiting colossal magnetoresistance (CMR), the paramagnetic insulating phase above the ferromagnetic Curie temperature T_c is conjectured to be inhomogeneous, containing nanometer-scale clusters with short-range charge and orbital order coexisting with ferromagnetic metallic regions.

Provide a set of experimental criteria — using a combination of complementary probes such as elastic and inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering, scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, electron microscopy, NMR, μSR, and pair distribution function analysis — that together would:

(a) unambiguously establish the existence of charge-ordered nanoclusters in the temperature regime T > T_c in CMR manganites;

(b) rule out any spatially homogeneous (single-phase) electronic explanation of the colossal magnetoresistance effect; and

(c) identify the specific spectroscopic signatures of such nanoclusters in the frequency-dependent optical conductivity σ(ω), distinguishing their contribution from the conventional small-polaron description (in which σ(ω) is modeled as arising from photon-assisted hopping of self-trapped carriers coupled to local lattice distortions, with a characteristic broad mid-infrared peak whose position scales with the polaron binding energy).

Specifically, determine how the presence of charge-ordered nanoclusters manifests itself in σ(ω): which spectral features (peak positions, spectral-weight transfers as a function of temperature and magnetic field, or sum-rule violations) are attributable to cluster formation rather than to isolated small polarons.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a physics research program rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Subsequent literature on CMR manganites (e.g., reviews by Dagotto, Tokura, and work on phase separation and nanoscale inhomogeneities through the 2000s–2020s) provides increasing evidence for nanoscale phase separation and charge-ordered correlations above T_c, but a definitive, universally accepted experimental ruling-out of homogeneous CMR scenarios and a complete attribution of optical-conductivity features to nanoclusters versus small polarons has not been achieved. The status is best characterized as open / partially addressed.

status_evidence.title: Phase separation in colossal magnetoresistance manganites (review)
status_evidence.snippet: Calls for further confirmation of charge-ordered nanoclusters above T_c and clarification of their role in optical conductivity beyond a small-polaron description.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as an open research question requiring multi-technique experimental confirmation.
